sectionTitle: Reactions of alkenes and alcohols (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Alkenes are hydrocarbons with a double carbon-carbon bond. The general formula for the homologous series of alkenes is Cₙ H₂ₙ
Alkene molecules are unsaturated because they contain two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.
The first four members of the homologous series of alkenes are ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
Alkene molecules can be represented in the following forms:
C₃ H₆
or
Students do not need to know the names of individual alkenes other than ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
Alkenes are hydrocarbons with the functional group C=C.
It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determine the reactions of organic compounds.
Alkenes react with oxygen in combustion reactions in the same way as other hydrocarbons, but they tend to burn in air with smoky flames because of incomplete combustion.
Alkenes react with hydrogen, water and the halogens, by the addition of atoms across the carbon-carbon double bond so that the double bond becomes a single carbon-carbon bond.
Students should be able to:
describe the reactions and conditions for the addition of hydrogen, water and halogens to alkenes
draw fully displayed structural formulae of the first four members of the alkenes and the products of their addition reactions with hydrogen, water, chlorine, bromine and iodine.
Alcohols contain the functional group –OH.
Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol are the first four members of a homologous series of alcohols.
Alcohols can be represented in the following forms:
CH₃ CH₂ OH
or
Students should be able to:
describe what happens when any of the first four alcohols react with sodium, burn in air, are added to water, react with an oxidising agent
recall the main uses of these alcohols.
Aqueous solutions of ethanol are produced when sugar solutions are fermented using yeast.
Students should know the conditions used for fermentation of sugar using yeast.
Students should be able to recognise alcohols from their names or from given formulae.
Students do not need to know the names of individual alcohols other than methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol.
Students are not expected to write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of alcohols other than for combustion reactions.
Carboxylic acids have the functional group –COOH.
The first four members of a homologous series of carboxylic acids are methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid.
The structures of carboxylic acids can be represented in the following forms:
CH₃ COOH
or
Students should be able to:
describe what happens when any of the first four carboxylic acids react with carbonates, dissolve in water, react with alcohols
(HT only) explain why carboxylic acids are weak acids in terms of ionisation and pH (see Strong and weak acids (HT only) ).
Students should be able to recognise carboxylic acids from their names or from given formulae.
Students do not need to know the names of individual carboxylic acids other than methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid.
Students are not expected to write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of carboxylic acids.
Students do not need to know the names of esters other than ethyl ethanoate.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of individual alkenes other than ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only ethene, propene, butene and pentene are named anywhere in this material. No alkene beyond pentene is named anywhere, in a concept, a correction or a question option, and no question asks a student to name an alkene from a formula or to place a name in the series beyond pentene. Where a general point about the series is made it is made through the general formula CₙH₂ₙ or through one of the four named members. Positional names such as but-1-ene and but-2-ene, and the idea that a double bond can sit in different places along a chain, are not introduced, because the specification asks for the names of these four members only.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of individual alcohols other than methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every alcohol students are asked to know, name or work with here is methanol, ethanol, propanol or butanol. Questions that ask students to recognise an alcohol do so from the –OH functional group or from one of those four names. A fifth member of the series appears once, only as a wrong option in a list question, where the point is recognising that it falls outside the required four; nothing asks a student to recall it, its formula or its reactions. Branched or multi-position alcohols, and names such as propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, are not used.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not expected to write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of alcohols other than for combustion reactions.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only balanced equation given or asked for in the alcohol material is a combustion equation, and one question tests exactly that. The reactions of alcohols with sodium, with water and with an oxidising agent are treated by description only: what is seen, what is produced and what the product is called. No item asks for a balanced equation, a formula equation or a state-symbol equation for those three reactions, and none is supplied in the concepts or corrections.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of individual carboxylic acids other than methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every carboxylic acid students are asked to know, name or work with here is methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic or butanoic acid, and recognition questions rely on the –COOH functional group or on those four names. A fifth member appears once, only as a wrong option in a list question, where the point is recognising that it falls outside the required four; nothing asks a student to recall it, its formula or its reactions.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not expected to write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of carboxylic acids.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No balanced equation appears anywhere in the carboxylic acid material. The reaction with carbonates is described by its observation and named products in words, dissolving in water is described by the pH of the solution formed, and the reaction with an alcohol is described by the name of the ester produced. No question option contains a symbol equation for a carboxylic acid reaction, and no correction supplies one.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of esters other than ethyl ethanoate.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Ethyl ethanoate is the only ester named in this material, and it appears only as the product of ethanoic acid reacting with ethanol. No other ester is named, no rule for building ester names from an acid and an alcohol is taught, and no item asks a student to name the ester formed from any other pair of reactants.

concepts.definition: A hydrocarbon with a double carbon–carbon bond. Being a hydrocarbon, it contains hydrogen and carbon atoms only; the C=C is what separates it from an alkane.
CₙH₂ₙ. For any member of the homologous series, the number of hydrogen atoms is twice the number of carbon atoms: C₂H₄, C₃H₆, C₄H₈, C₅H₁₀. The alkanes, by contrast, are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

The word used for alkene molecules because they contain two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms. The double bond means the molecule is not carrying as many hydrogen atoms as that many carbon atoms could hold.
The exact comparison the specification makes. Propane is C₃H₈ and propene is C₃H₆; butane is C₄H₁₀ and butene is C₄H₈. Same carbon count, two hydrogen atoms fewer.
Ethene, propene, butene and pentene, in that order: C₂H₄, C₃H₆, C₄H₈ and C₅H₁₀. The series starts at two carbon atoms because a carbon–carbon double bond needs two carbon atoms to exist.
A form in which an alkene molecule can be represented, giving the number of atoms of each element in one molecule. It says nothing about which atoms are joined to which.
The molecular formula of propene: three carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms in one molecule. It fits CₙH₂ₙ, and it is two hydrogen atoms short of propane, C₃H₈.

The alternative form in which an alkene molecule can be represented, showing every atom and every bond, with two lines drawn between the two carbon atoms joined by the double bond. Propene drawn this way is CH₂=CH–CH₃ with all six C–H bonds shown.
The carbon–carbon double bond that alkenes contain. It is the part of the molecule where reaction happens, and it is what all alkenes have in common.

It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determines the reactions of organic compounds. Because ethene, propene, butene and pentene all carry a C=C, they all undergo the same kinds of reaction, so what is learned for one alkene applies to the others.
Alkenes react with oxygen in combustion reactions in the same way as other hydrocarbons, but they tend to burn in air with smoky flames. The smoke is a sign of incomplete combustion.

The reaction of an alkene with hydrogen, water or a halogen, in which atoms are added across the carbon–carbon double bond. Nothing is removed from the alkene: the whole of the added molecule joins on.
In an addition reaction the double bond becomes a single carbon–carbon bond. The two carbon atoms stay joined to each other, but each now holds one extra atom, so the product is saturated.

An alkene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst. One hydrogen atom adds to each of the two carbon atoms of the C=C, and the product is the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms: ethene gives ethane, propene gives propane.
An alkene reacts with water in the form of steam, in the presence of a catalyst. The water adds across the double bond and the product is an alcohol: ethene gives ethanol, propene gives propanol.
An alkene reacts with chlorine, bromine or iodine without a catalyst being needed. One halogen atom adds to each of the two carbon atoms of the C=C, so ethene and bromine give C₂H₄Br₂.

In the product of an addition reaction the two lines between the carbon atoms are replaced by one, and the new atom on each of those carbon atoms is drawn in with its bond. Ethene plus chlorine gives a molecule with a single C–C bond, four C–H bonds and two C–Cl bonds.
A compound containing the functional group –OH. The oxygen and hydrogen of that group are joined to the rest of the molecule by ordinary bonds; the group is not a hydroxide ion.
Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol, the first four members of a homologous series: CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH and C₄H₉OH. Each has one more carbon atom than the one before.
A form in which ethanol can be represented. It shows two carbon atoms, the hydrogen atoms attached to them, and the –OH group written last so that the functional group can be seen.

The alternative form, showing every atom and every bond, including the C–O bond and the O–H bond of the functional group. For ethanol that is two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, five C–H bonds, one C–O bond and one O–H bond.
A piece of sodium added to any of the first four alcohols fizzes as hydrogen gas is given off, and the sodium is used up. The gas is hydrogen, not oxygen and not carbon dioxide.
The first four alcohols burn in air. In complete combustion the products are carbon dioxide and water, for example C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O for ethanol.
The first four alcohols dissolve in water, and the solution formed is neutral. Having an –OH group does not make an alcohol either an acid or an alkali.
An alcohol reacted with an oxidising agent is oxidised to a carboxylic acid. Ethanol gives ethanoic acid, which is why wine left open to the air turns sour.
The first four alcohols are used as fuels and as solvents, and ethanol is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks. Methanol has the fuel and solvent uses but is not drunk.
The process in which aqueous solutions of ethanol are produced when sugar solutions are fermented using yeast. The ethanol is produced in solution, mixed with water, rather than as a pure liquid.
Yeast, sugar dissolved in water, a warm temperature of about 30 °C, and the absence of oxygen. Too cold and the process is very slow; too hot and the yeast is killed.

An alcohol is recognised from a name ending in –ol, such as methanol or butanol, or from a formula in which an –OH group is written on the end of a hydrocarbon chain, such as C₃H₇OH. A formula ending in –COOH is a carboxylic acid, not an alcohol.
A compound containing the functional group –COOH. That group contains a carbon atom, two oxygen atoms and a hydrogen atom, and it is what makes the compound acidic.
Methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid, the first four members of a homologous series: HCOOH, CH₃COOH, C₂H₅COOH and C₃H₇COOH.
A form in which ethanoic acid can be represented. Two carbon atoms in all: three hydrogen atoms sit on the first, and the second carbon atom carries the –COOH group.

concepts.term: Displayed formula of a carboxylic acid
concepts.definition: The alternative form, showing every atom and every bond, including the double bond from carbon to one oxygen atom and the single O–H bond in the –COOH group.
A carboxylic acid added to a carbonate fizzes, and the gas given off is carbon dioxide. This is the same behaviour as any acid with a carbonate.
The first four carboxylic acids dissolve in water to give acidic solutions, with a pH below 7.
A carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol to produce an ester. Ethanoic acid and ethanol give the ester ethyl ethanoate.

A carboxylic acid is a weak acid because it does not ionise completely in water: only a small proportion of its molecules release hydrogen ions. The concentration of hydrogen ions is therefore lower, and the pH higher, than for a solution of a strong acid of the same concentration.
A carboxylic acid is recognised from a name ending in –oic acid, such as ethanoic acid, or from a formula ending in –COOH, such as C₂H₅COOH. Methanoic acid, with one carbon atom in total, is HCOOH.

misconceptions.question: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkenes?
misconceptions.correct: CₙH₂ₙ. Propene is C₃H₆ and butene is C₄H₈.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkenes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, the same as the alkanes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alkanes are met first and their general formula is drilled hard, so CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ becomes the formula students reach for whenever a hydrocarbon series is mentioned.
misconceptions.correction: The two series have different general formulae. Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and alkenes are CₙH₂ₙ. Checking a known member settles it: propene is C₃H₆, which is 2 × 3 hydrogen atoms, not 2 × 3 + 2.

misconceptions.question: Propane is C₃H₈. How many hydrogen atoms does propene have?
misconceptions.correct: Six. Propene is C₃H₆, two fewer hydrogen atoms than propane.
misconceptions.misconception: An unsaturated molecule has more hydrogen atoms than the saturated one, because 'unsaturated' sounds like there is room for extra.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday sense of 'saturated' is soaked or full up, so students expect the unsaturated one to be the emptier of the two and then muddle which way the atom count moves.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states it directly: alkene molecules are unsaturated because they contain two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms. Unsaturated means fewer hydrogen atoms, not more.

misconceptions.question: What is the first member of the homologous series of alkenes?
misconceptions.correct: Ethene. The first four are ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
misconceptions.misconception: The first alkene is 'methene', because the first alkane is methane and the two series must line up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students pattern-match the alkene names onto the alkane names they already know, and methane is the obvious starting point of that list.
misconceptions.correction: The series starts at ethene because an alkene must contain a carbon–carbon double bond, and a molecule with only one carbon atom has no second carbon atom to double bond to. There is no such compound as methene.

misconceptions.question: Does the molecular formula C₃H₆ show you where the double bond is?
misconceptions.correct: No. It gives only the number of atoms of each element; the displayed formula is what shows the bonds.
misconceptions.misconception: A molecular formula shows the structure of the molecule, so C₃H₆ tells you which atoms are joined to which.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both forms are called 'the formula', and both are written with the same element symbols, so students treat them as the same information written two ways.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives two forms because they carry different information. C₃H₆ counts atoms. The displayed formula shows every atom and every bond, including the two lines between the double-bonded carbon atoms.

misconceptions.question: Does the double bond make an alkene less reactive than an alkane?
misconceptions.correct: No. The C=C is the functional group, and it is where alkenes react.
misconceptions.misconception: A double bond is two bonds instead of one, so it is stronger and harder to break, which makes alkenes unreactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that breaking bonds needs energy and then reason that more bonds must mean a more inert molecule, without meeting the idea that a functional group is a site of reaction.
misconceptions.correction: The specification treats C=C as the functional group of the alkenes, and functional groups determine reactions. Alkenes react with hydrogen, water and the halogens by addition across that bond, which is a reaction alkanes do not undergo.

misconceptions.question: If you know how ethene reacts with bromine, do you have to learn propene separately?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both contain C=C, so both react in the same way.
misconceptions.misconception: Every alkene has its own separate list of reactions that has to be learned one by one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Organic chemistry looks like a long list of names, so students expect a long list of unrelated facts rather than one rule applied repeatedly.
misconceptions.correction: It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determines the reactions of organic compounds. Every alkene carries the same C=C, so the same addition reactions apply across the series.

misconceptions.question: Why do alkenes tend to burn in air with smoky flames?
misconceptions.correct: Because combustion is incomplete.
misconceptions.misconception: The smoky flame shows that the alkene is burning very well, giving out a lot of carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A big bright yellow flame looks more impressive than a small blue one, so students read 'smoky' as a sign of a vigorous, complete burn.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says alkenes tend to burn in air with smoky flames because of incomplete combustion. The smoke is unburnt carbon: not all of the fuel has been fully oxidised.

misconceptions.question: In the reaction of ethene with bromine, is a hydrogen atom replaced?
misconceptions.correct: No. Bromine atoms add on across the double bond and no hydrogen is lost.
misconceptions.misconception: The bromine swaps places with a hydrogen atom on the alkene, so hydrogen bromide is given off.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Substitution is the first organic reaction type many students meet, and any reaction of a hydrocarbon with a halogen is then assumed to work the same way.
misconceptions.correction: The specification describes these as reactions by the addition of atoms across the carbon–carbon double bond. The whole of the added molecule joins on, nothing leaves the alkene, and the product of ethene with bromine is C₂H₄Br₂.

misconceptions.question: After hydrogen has added to ethene, is there still a C=C in the product?
misconceptions.correct: No. The double bond has become a single carbon–carbon bond.
misconceptions.misconception: The atoms just attach onto the molecule and the double bond stays where it was.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture addition as sticking something onto the outside of a molecule that is otherwise unchanged, so nothing inside the molecule seems to need to move.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says atoms add across the carbon–carbon double bond so that the double bond becomes a single carbon–carbon bond. One of the two bonds between the carbon atoms is used to hold the new atoms, so the product is saturated.

misconceptions.question: What happens if you shake an alkene with cold water?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing useful. The addition of water needs steam and a catalyst.
misconceptions.misconception: You make an alcohol simply by adding water to an alkene at room temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word equation 'alkene + water → alcohol' is memorised without its conditions, and mixing two liquids is what 'adding water' looks like in the lab.
misconceptions.correction: The specification asks for the reactions and the conditions. Water is added as steam and a catalyst is used; the reaction does not happen just by mixing an alkene with cold water.

misconceptions.question: Does bromine need a catalyst to react with an alkene?
misconceptions.correct: No. Halogens add across the double bond without a catalyst being needed.
misconceptions.misconception: All of the addition reactions of alkenes need a catalyst, because the hydrogen one does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conditions are learned as a single block for 'addition reactions', so the catalyst needed for hydrogen is carried over to every reagent.
misconceptions.correction: The conditions differ by reagent. Hydrogen needs a catalyst and water is added as steam with a catalyst, but chlorine, bromine and iodine add to alkenes readily without one.

misconceptions.question: What must a fully displayed structural formula show?
misconceptions.correct: Every atom and every bond in the molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: A displayed formula only needs to show the carbon atoms and the double bond; the hydrogen atoms can be left off.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see skeletal-looking sketches on whiteboards and in hurried notes, and take the shortcut for the real thing.
misconceptions.correction: The specification asks for fully displayed structural formulae. Every hydrogen atom must be drawn, and every bond must be drawn as a line, including all the C–H bonds and both lines of a C=C.

misconceptions.question: Ethanol contains an –OH group. Is its solution in water alkaline?
misconceptions.correct: No. Alcohols dissolve in water to give neutral solutions.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything containing OH is a hydroxide, so an alcohol dissolved in water must be alkaline and turn universal indicator blue.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium hydroxide, NaOH, is met long before organic chemistry, and the letters OH are strongly associated with alkalis from that point on.
misconceptions.correction: The –OH in an alcohol is a covalently bonded functional group, not a hydroxide ion. Alcohols added to water dissolve and the solution formed is neutral.

misconceptions.question: Does CH₃CH₂OH contain a hydroxide ion?
misconceptions.correct: No. The oxygen and hydrogen are bonded into the molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: The OH written at the end of CH₃CH₂OH is an OH⁻ ion attached to the rest of the molecule.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae such as NaOH and Ca(OH)₂ really do contain hydroxide ions, and the same three characters appear at the end of an alcohol formula.
misconceptions.correction: Alcohols are molecular, not ionic. In CH₃CH₂OH the oxygen atom is joined to a carbon atom by one bond and to a hydrogen atom by another; there are no ions in the molecule to be released.

misconceptions.question: Which gas is given off when sodium reacts with ethanol?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxygen is given off, because the –OH group is where the oxygen in the molecule is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for the product inside the reactant formula and see an oxygen atom sitting right next to the reactive site.
misconceptions.correction: The gas is hydrogen. Sodium reacting with an alcohol behaves like sodium reacting with water: the metal displaces hydrogen from the –OH group, and the alcohol's oxygen stays in solution as part of the other product.

misconceptions.question: What is produced when ethanol burns completely in air?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide and water.
misconceptions.misconception: Burning ethanol turns it into ethanoic acid, because burning is a kind of oxidation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid and that combustion is oxidation, and merge the two into one reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Combustion and oxidation by an oxidising agent give different products. Burned in air, ethanol gives carbon dioxide and water; warmed with an oxidising agent, it gives ethanoic acid.

misconceptions.question: What is formed when ethanol reacts with an oxidising agent?
misconceptions.correct: Ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid.
misconceptions.misconception: An oxidising agent oxidises ethanol all the way to carbon dioxide and water, just like burning it does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Oxidised' is first met in the context of burning and rusting, where carbon ends up as carbon dioxide, so students expect the same end point every time.
misconceptions.correction: An oxidising agent takes the alcohol one step, to the carboxylic acid. Ethanol becomes ethanoic acid, which is what makes wine left open to the air taste sour.

misconceptions.question: Apart from alcoholic drinks, what are alcohols used for?
misconceptions.correct: As fuels and as solvents.
misconceptions.misconception: Alcohols are only used for making alcoholic drinks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of the word 'alcohol' is a drink, and that meaning arrives years before the chemical one.
misconceptions.correction: The main uses of the first four alcohols are as fuels and as solvents, as well as ethanol's use in alcoholic drinks. Methanol is used as a fuel and a solvent but is toxic and is never drunk.

misconceptions.question: Is fermentation faster if the mixture is made really hot?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fermentation needs a warm temperature of about 30 °C.
misconceptions.misconception: The hotter the mixture the better, because reactions always speed up when they are heated.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rate-of-reaction rule that heating speeds a reaction up is applied without exception, and students do not connect fermentation to enzymes in living yeast.
misconceptions.correction: Fermentation depends on enzymes in yeast. Warmth speeds it up only up to a point; too hot and the enzymes are denatured and the yeast is killed, so the process stops. About 30 °C is used.

misconceptions.question: Is CH₃COOH an alcohol, since it contains an O and an H?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its functional group is –COOH, so it is a carboxylic acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Any formula containing oxygen and hydrogen together is an alcohol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn to spot 'OH' at the end of a formula as the sign of an alcohol, and the last two characters of CH₃COOH are O and H.
misconceptions.correction: What matters is the whole functional group, not the letters. An alcohol has –OH joined to a carbon chain; in CH₃COOH the carbon atom carries two oxygen atoms, making –COOH, the carboxylic acid group.

misconceptions.question: The –COOH group contains an O–H bond. Does that make a carboxylic acid an alcohol?
misconceptions.correct: No. The functional group of a carboxylic acid is the whole of –COOH.
misconceptions.misconception: Carboxylic acids are a kind of alcohol, because –COOH has an –OH inside it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The –OH is genuinely there in the drawn structure, so the group looks like an alcohol with something extra bolted on.
misconceptions.correction: A functional group is taken as a whole. In –COOH the O–H sits on a carbon atom that also carries a C=O, and that combination behaves completely differently from an alcohol: it dissolves to give an acidic solution and it fizzes with carbonates.

misconceptions.question: Do all four hydrogen atoms in CH₃COOH ionise in water?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the hydrogen atom in the –COOH group can ionise, and even that only partly.
misconceptions.misconception: Every hydrogen atom in an acid molecule is released as an H⁺ ion in solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acids are introduced as sources of H⁺ ions, so any hydrogen atom in the formula of an acid looks like a potential H⁺.
misconceptions.correction: Only the hydrogen in the –COOH group is acidic, and because a carboxylic acid is weak it does not ionise completely: at any moment only a small proportion of those molecules have released their hydrogen ion.

misconceptions.question: Which gas is given off when ethanoic acid is added to a carbonate?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen is given off, because acids give off hydrogen when they fizz.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acid plus metal producing hydrogen is usually the first fizzing reaction students meet, so hydrogen becomes the default answer for any acid that bubbles.
misconceptions.correction: It depends on what the acid is reacting with. Acid with a metal gives hydrogen; acid with a carbonate gives carbon dioxide. A carboxylic acid with a carbonate gives carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.question: What is produced when ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol?
misconceptions.correct: An ester, ethyl ethanoate.
misconceptions.misconception: An acid plus an alcohol gives a salt and water, because that is what acids do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutralisation is drilled as 'acid + base → salt + water', and an alcohol with its –OH group looks close enough to a base to trigger the rule.
misconceptions.correction: Alcohols are not bases and this is not neutralisation. A carboxylic acid reacting with an alcohol produces an ester; ethanoic acid with ethanol gives ethyl ethanoate.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean to call ethanoic acid a weak acid?
misconceptions.correct: That it does not ionise completely in water; only a small proportion of its molecules release hydrogen ions.
misconceptions.misconception: A weak acid is simply a dilute acid, and a strong acid is a concentrated one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech weak and dilute mean the same thing about a drink, and both pairs of words are used about acids in the same lesson.
misconceptions.correction: Strength and concentration are separate ideas. Concentration is how much acid is dissolved in a given volume; strength is what proportion of the acid molecules ionise. A carboxylic acid can be concentrated and still weak.

misconceptions.question: Hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid have the same concentration. Which has the higher pH?
misconceptions.correct: Ethanoic acid, because it is weak and so has a lower concentration of hydrogen ions.
misconceptions.misconception: A weak acid must have a pH of 7 or above, because it barely ionises.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat 'weak' as meaning 'hardly an acid at all', and the only pH they can then attach to it is the neutral one.
misconceptions.correction: A weak acid still ionises to some extent, so its solution is still acidic and its pH is still below 7. It is higher than that of a strong acid of the same concentration, but it does not reach 7.

misconceptions.question: What is the formula of methanoic acid?
misconceptions.correct: HCOOH. It has one carbon atom in the whole molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: Methanoic acid is CH₃COOH, because the acid group is added onto a methyl group.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn ethanoic acid as CH₃COOH first and then build the name-formula link the wrong way round, treating CH₃ as the 'meth' part.
misconceptions.correction: The stem counts every carbon atom, including the one in –COOH. Methanoic acid has one carbon atom in total, so it is HCOOH; ethanoic acid has two, so it is CH₃COOH.

misconceptions.question: Propanol and propanoic acid both start with 'propan'. Are they the same kind of compound?
misconceptions.correct: No. Propanol is an alcohol and propanoic acid is a carboxylic acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Names that share a stem belong to the same homologous series, so propanol and propanoic acid must behave alike.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The shared stem is the loudest part of the name, and students read the ending as decoration rather than as the part that names the functional group.
misconceptions.correction: The stem gives the number of carbon atoms; the ending gives the functional group. –ol means –OH and –oic acid means –COOH, and those two groups give completely different reactions.

misconceptions.question: Do alkanes and alkenes react in the same ways because both are hydrocarbons?
misconceptions.correct: No. Their reactions are determined by their functional groups, and alkenes have a C=C.
misconceptions.misconception: All hydrocarbons behave the same way, so alkenes react exactly like alkanes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Hydrocarbon' is taught as one category, and students expect one category to mean one set of properties.
misconceptions.correction: It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determines the reactions of organic compounds. The C=C of an alkene allows addition reactions with hydrogen, water and the halogens, which alkanes do not undergo.

misconceptions.question: A smoky flame leaves black solid on a dish. Where has the black solid come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the fuel, as unburnt carbon produced by incomplete combustion.
misconceptions.misconception: The black solid was already there as soot inside the alkene before it was lit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Soot looks like a substance that has simply been released rather than made, and students do not connect the black solid to the way the fuel burned.
misconceptions.correction: The carbon was chemically part of the alkene, not present as soot. When there is not enough oxygen for complete combustion, some of that carbon is released as solid carbon instead of being oxidised to carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.question: When chlorine adds to ethene, how many chlorine atoms join on?
misconceptions.correct: Two, one to each of the carbon atoms of the double bond.
misconceptions.misconception: Only one chlorine atom joins on, because only one bond of the double bond breaks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students count one bond becoming available and match one atom to it, without noticing that the two carbon atoms each need a new partner.
misconceptions.correction: Breaking one of the two bonds between the carbon atoms leaves both of those carbon atoms able to bond to something new, so one atom adds to each. Ethene and chlorine give C₂H₄Cl₂.

misconceptions.question: When balancing the combustion of ethanol, does the oxygen atom in C₂H₅OH count?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. It must be included with the oxygen from the air.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the O₂ from the air counts as oxygen when you balance a combustion equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In alkane combustion the fuel contains no oxygen, so students form the habit of balancing oxygen from the O₂ alone and carry it over to alcohols.
misconceptions.correction: Every atom in the equation must balance, including the oxygen atom in the alcohol. For ethanol there are seven oxygen atoms on each side: one from C₂H₅OH and six from 3O₂ gives 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.

misconceptions.question: How many hydrogen atoms does C₂H₅OH contain?
misconceptions.correct: Six: five on the carbon atoms and one in the –OH group.
misconceptions.misconception: Ethanol has five hydrogen atoms, since the H in the –OH belongs with the oxygen and is counted separately.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The formula is written in two chunks and students total up only the chunk that looks like a hydrocarbon.
misconceptions.correction: The molecular formula of ethanol is C₂H₆O. The hydrogen atom in the –OH group is part of the molecule and must be counted, which matters whenever a combustion equation is balanced.

misconceptions.question: A reaction fizzes. Does that mean carbon dioxide is being produced?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fizzing only tells you that a gas is being produced.
misconceptions.misconception: Any fizzing in a reaction means carbon dioxide is being given off.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbonate reactions are the fizzing reactions students see most often, and the gas test they remember best is limewater for carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.correction: The gas has to be identified from the chemistry, not from the bubbles. Sodium with an alcohol fizzes because hydrogen is produced; a carboxylic acid with a carbonate fizzes because carbon dioxide is produced.

misconceptions.question: Does fermentation need air bubbled through the mixture?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fermentation is carried out in the absence of oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: Yeast is alive, so it needs a supply of air to make ethanol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know living things respire and need oxygen, and apply that to yeast without meeting the idea that fermentation is what yeast does when oxygen is absent.
misconceptions.correction: The conditions for fermentation are yeast, sugar in solution, a warm temperature of about 30 °C and the absence of oxygen. If air is supplied the ethanol produced is oxidised and the yield falls.

misconceptions.question: Can methanol be drunk in the same way as ethanol?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ethanol is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks; methanol is toxic.
misconceptions.misconception: All alcohols can be drunk, because alcohol is the stuff in drinks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'alcohol' names a whole homologous series in chemistry but names one particular drink ingredient in everyday life.
misconceptions.correction: Only ethanol is used in alcoholic drinks. Methanol, propanol and butanol share the –OH functional group and are used as fuels and solvents, but they are not drunk.

mcqs.stem: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkenes?

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
options.rationale: The general formula of the alkanes, reached for by students who learned it first and apply it to any hydrocarbon series.

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
options.rationale: Comes from taking 'two fewer hydrogen atoms' and subtracting the two from 2n instead of from the alkane's 2n + 2.

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ
options.rationale: This is the general formula the specification gives for the alkenes: twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms, as in C₃H₆.

options.text: CₙHₙ
options.rationale: Picked by students who assume a double bond means one hydrogen atom per carbon atom rather than two.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a correct description of an alkene?

options.text: A hydrocarbon in which all the carbon bonds are single
options.rationale: This describes an alkane, and is chosen by students who have not separated the two series.

options.text: A hydrocarbon that is unreactive because of its strong bond
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read a double bond as two bonds to break and therefore as a barrier to reaction.

options.text: A compound containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms
options.rationale: Confuses alkenes with alcohols; an alkene is a hydrocarbon and contains no oxygen.

options.text: A hydrocarbon that contains a carbon–carbon double bond
options.rationale: The specification defines alkenes as hydrocarbons with a double carbon-carbon bond.

mcqs.stem: Propane has the formula C₃H₈. What is the formula of propene?

options.text: C₃H₆
options.rationale: Propene is unsaturated: it has two fewer hydrogen atoms than propane, the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.

options.text: C₃H₈
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think alkanes and alkenes with the same carbon count share a formula.

options.text: C₃H₁₀
options.rationale: Comes from reading 'unsaturated' as having room for extra hydrogen, so two are added rather than removed.

options.text: C₃H₄
options.rationale: Results from removing two hydrogen molecules rather than two hydrogen atoms.

mcqs.stem: Why is propene described as unsaturated?

options.text: It has more hydrogen atoms than the alkane with three carbon atoms
options.rationale: The everyday sense of 'saturated' as full leads students to move the hydrogen count the wrong way.

options.text: It has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with three carbons
options.rationale: This is the specification's own reason: alkene molecules contain two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.

options.text: Its double bond means that it cannot take part in any reactions
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat the double bond as a stronger, unreactive link rather than a functional group.

options.text: It has fewer carbon atoms than the alkane it was originally made from
options.rationale: Confuses unsaturation with cracking; the carbon count is unchanged between propane and propene.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives the first four members of the homologous series of alkenes?

options.text: methene, ethene, propene, butene
options.rationale: Chosen by students who line the alkenes up with the alkanes and start the series at a one-carbon member.

options.text: ethane, propane, butane, pentane
options.rationale: These are alkanes; picked by students who have not separated the -ane and -ene endings.

options.text: ethene, propene, butene, pentene
options.rationale: These are the four alkenes named in the specification, in order of increasing carbon number.

options.text: ethene, ethane, propene, propane
options.rationale: Alternates alkenes with alkanes; chosen by students who have not fixed the -ene ending as the marker of an alkene.

mcqs.stem: An alkene molecule can be represented by a molecular formula such as C₃H₆. What does that form tell you?

options.text: Which pair of carbon atoms the double bond joins
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat every formula as showing structure.

options.text: Only the carbon skeleton, leaving the hydrogens out
options.rationale: Comes from students who confuse the two representations and think hydrogen is left off.

options.text: The shape of the molecule in three dimensions
options.rationale: Neither representation in the specification shows three-dimensional shape.

options.text: The number of atoms of each element in one molecule
options.rationale: A molecular formula counts atoms; that is all it does.

mcqs.stem: Which of these formulae fits the general formula CₙH₂ₙ?

options.text: C₄H₁₀
options.rationale: Fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, the alkane formula, chosen by students working from the series they learned first.

options.text: C₄H₈
options.rationale: With n = 4, 2n = 8, so this fits CₙH₂ₙ and is the formula of butene.

options.text: C₅H₈
options.rationale: Comes from subtracting two hydrogen atoms from 2n rather than from the alkane formula.

options.text: C₂H₆
options.rationale: Has three hydrogen atoms per carbon atom, so it does not fit; a student may check only that H exceeds C.

mcqs.stem: Propene can also be represented by a fully displayed formula. What does that form show that C₃H₆ does not?

options.text: Which atoms are joined together and where the double bond is
options.rationale: A displayed formula draws every atom and every bond, so it shows the position of the C=C.

options.text: How many hydrogen atoms one molecule of propene contains
options.rationale: This is what the molecular formula already gives, so it cannot be the extra information.

options.text: How many carbon atoms there are in the main chain
options.rationale: Also given by C₃H₆; chosen by students unsure what a displayed formula adds.

options.text: How much energy is given out when propene is burned
options.rationale: No structural representation carries energy data; picked by students guessing at extra detail.

mcqs.stem: What is the functional group of the alkenes?

options.text: C–C
options.rationale: Chosen by students who do not distinguish the double bond from an ordinary single carbon-carbon bond.

options.text: –OH
options.rationale: The alcohol functional group, picked by students who mix up the groups of the different series.

options.text: C=C
options.rationale: The specification states that alkenes are hydrocarbons with the functional group C=C.

options.text: –COOH
options.rationale: The carboxylic acid functional group, offered here to catch the same confusion between series.

mcqs.stem: Ethene, propene and butene all react with bromine in the same way. What best explains this?

options.text: Each alkene happens to have its own matching reaction
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat organic chemistry as a list of separate facts rather than one rule.

options.text: They all contain the same functional group, C=C
options.rationale: It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determines the reactions of organic compounds.

options.text: They all contain the same number of carbon atoms
options.rationale: Factually wrong: the three alkenes differ in carbon number, which is the point of a homologous series.

options.text: All hydrocarbons react in the same way as each other
options.rationale: Comes from treating 'hydrocarbon' as a single category with one set of reactions.

mcqs.stem: How do alkenes tend to burn in air?

options.text: With a smoky flame, because combustion is complete
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read a big smoky flame as a sign of vigorous, complete burning.

options.text: With a clean blue flame, exactly as alkanes do in air
options.rationale: Comes from assuming all hydrocarbons burn identically.

options.text: They do not burn in air at all, because of the C=C
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the double bond makes an alkene unreactive.

options.text: With a smoky flame, because combustion is incomplete
options.rationale: The specification says alkenes tend to burn in air with smoky flames because of incomplete combustion.

mcqs.stem: A student burns ethene in air. The flame is yellow and smoky, and black solid collects on a dish held above it. What does this show?

options.text: The ethene has burned completely to carbon dioxide and water
options.rationale: Chosen by students who take a large smoky flame as evidence of complete combustion.

options.text: Not all of the ethene has been fully oxidised to carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Solid carbon is deposited when combustion is incomplete, which is why alkenes burn with smoky flames.

options.text: The ethene already contained particles of soot before burning
options.rationale: Treats the black solid as something released rather than something produced by the reaction.

options.text: The dish above the flame was too cold for ethene to burn well
options.rationale: Blames the apparatus; the smoky flame is a property of the fuel burning in a limited oxygen supply.

mcqs.stem: In the addition of hydrogen to an alkene, what happens to the carbon–carbon double bond?

options.text: It stays as a double bond in the product
options.rationale: Chosen by students who picture addition as sticking atoms onto an unchanged molecule.

options.text: It becomes a single carbon–carbon bond
options.rationale: The specification says the double bond becomes a single carbon-carbon bond when atoms add across it.

options.text: It breaks and the two carbon atoms separate
options.rationale: Comes from thinking that breaking a bond must split the molecule in two.

options.text: It turns into a triple carbon–carbon bond
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume adding atoms must add bonds between the carbon atoms as well.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is true of the addition reactions of alkenes?

options.text: Atoms replace hydrogen atoms already on the alkene
options.rationale: Substitution, the reaction type students meet first, wrongly applied to an alkene.

options.text: Atoms add on and the double bond is still present
options.rationale: Chosen by students who do not see that a bond must be given up to hold the new atoms.

options.text: Atoms add on and the carbon chain gets longer
options.rationale: Confuses addition to a double bond with joining molecules end to end.

options.text: Atoms add across the double bond, which becomes single
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of how alkenes react with hydrogen, water and the halogens.

mcqs.stem: What conditions are needed for hydrogen to add to an alkene?

options.text: The alkene and hydrogen react on mixing, with no catalyst
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume the conditions for halogen addition apply to hydrogen too.

options.text: The alkene is dissolved in water and the mixture is heated
options.rationale: Comes from muddling the addition of hydrogen with the addition of water.

options.text: The mixture is warmed with an oxidising agent added to it
options.rationale: Imports the oxidising agent used with alcohols into a reaction where it plays no part.

options.text: The alkene and hydrogen are passed over a catalyst
options.rationale: The addition of hydrogen to an alkene is carried out in the presence of a catalyst.

mcqs.stem: Ethene is reacted with steam in the presence of a catalyst. What is produced?

options.text: ethanoic acid, because the ethene has been oxidised
options.rationale: Confuses addition of water with oxidation by an oxidising agent.

options.text: ethanol, because water adds across the double bond
options.rationale: Water adds across the C=C, giving the alcohol with the same number of carbon atoms.

options.text: a solution of ethene in water, since ethene dissolves
options.rationale: Treats 'adding water' as mixing rather than as a reaction across the double bond.

options.text: ethene and steam, because the mixture does not react
options.rationale: Chosen by students who do not accept that the double bond can be changed.

mcqs.stem: How does bromine react with an alkene?

options.text: It adds across the double bond only if a catalyst is used
options.rationale: Applies the catalyst needed for hydrogen to every addition reaction.

options.text: It adds across the double bond without a catalyst
options.rationale: Halogens add readily across the C=C; no catalyst is needed, unlike the addition of hydrogen.

options.text: It replaces a hydrogen atom on one of the carbon atoms
options.rationale: Substitution, wrongly carried over from the reactions of alkanes with halogens.

options.text: It reacts only when the mixture is heated very strongly
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume every organic reaction needs strong heating.

mcqs.stem: Ethene reacts with chlorine. What is the formula of the product?

options.text: C₂H₃Cl
options.rationale: The substitution product: a chlorine atom has replaced a hydrogen atom instead of adding on.

options.text: C₂H₄Cl
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think only one chlorine atom can join because only one bond breaks.

options.text: C₂H₆Cl₂
options.rationale: Comes from adding chlorine to ethane rather than to ethene.

options.text: C₂H₄Cl₂
options.rationale: One chlorine atom adds to each carbon atom of the double bond, so both chlorine atoms join on and no hydrogen is lost.

mcqs.stem: Propene reacts with hydrogen. How many hydrogen atoms are shown in the fully displayed formula of the product?

options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the hydrogen simply attaches without changing the count in the formula.
Comes from adding only one hydrogen atom, on the assumption that only one bond becomes available.
Propene, C₃H₆, gains two hydrogen atoms across the double bond to give propane, C₃H₈.
Comes from adding two hydrogen molecules, four atoms in all, instead of two hydrogen atoms across the double bond.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is true of all of the first four alcohols?

options.text: Each contains the functional group –OH
options.rationale: The specification states that alcohols contain the functional group -OH.

options.text: Each contains the group –COOH as well
options.rationale: Confuses the alcohol group with the carboxylic acid group.

options.text: Each contains hydroxide ions, so is alkaline
options.rationale: Reads the letters OH as the hydroxide ion met in NaOH.

options.text: Each contains a carbon–carbon double bond
options.rationale: Imports the alkene functional group into the alcohols.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives the first four members of the homologous series of alcohols?

options.text: ethanol, propanol, butanol, pentanol
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect every series to begin at the two-carbon member, as the alkenes do.

options.text: methanoic, ethanoic, propanol, butanol
options.rationale: Mixes carboxylic acid names into the alcohols because the stems are shared.

options.text: methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol
options.rationale: These are the four alcohols named in the specification, in order of increasing carbon number.

options.text: methane, ethanol, propanol, butanol
options.rationale: Begins with the alkane methane, from students who confuse the -ane and -ol endings.

mcqs.stem: Ethanol can be represented as CH₃CH₂OH. What does this representation show?

options.text: A separate hydroxide ion joined onto the molecule
options.rationale: Treats the -OH as the OH- ion familiar from NaOH.

options.text: Two carbon atoms, with an –OH group on one of them
options.rationale: The formula is written so that the functional group can be picked out at the end of the chain.

options.text: An acid group, because the formula contains oxygen
options.rationale: Chosen by students who take any oxygen-containing organic formula to be an acid.

options.text: A carbon–carbon double bond between the two carbons
options.rationale: Reads CH₃CH₂ as if it were an alkene chain.

mcqs.stem: A displayed formula of ethanol is drawn instead of writing CH₃CH₂OH. What does the drawing add?

options.text: It shows the carbon atoms but not the hydrogen atoms
options.rationale: The common shortcut of leaving hydrogen atoms off a drawn structure.

options.text: It shows how many atoms of each element are present
options.rationale: That information is already in CH₃CH₂OH, so it cannot be what the drawing adds.

options.text: It shows the charge carried by each atom present
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe an alcohol contains ions.

options.text: It shows every atom and every bond in the molecule
options.rationale: A fully displayed structural formula draws all atoms and all bonds, including the O-H bond.

mcqs.stem: A small piece of sodium is added to ethanol. What is observed and produced?

options.text: It fizzes, and the gas given off is hydrogen
options.rationale: Sodium reacts with the -OH group of an alcohol, releasing hydrogen gas.

options.text: It fizzes, and the gas given off is oxygen
options.rationale: Chosen by students who look for the oxygen atom in the -OH group and expect it to be released.

options.text: It fizzes, and the gas is carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Comes from treating any fizzing reaction as producing carbon dioxide.

options.text: Nothing happens, as ethanol is unreactive
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect organic liquids to be inert towards metals.

mcqs.stem: Ethanol burns completely in air. What are the products?

options.text: ethanoic acid and water only
options.rationale: Merges combustion with oxidation by an oxidising agent.

options.text: carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect the hydrogen in the fuel to be released as a gas rather than ending up in water.

options.text: carbon monoxide and water
options.rationale: The incomplete combustion product, chosen by students who do not separate complete from incomplete burning.

options.text: carbon dioxide and water only
options.rationale: Complete combustion of an alcohol gives carbon dioxide and water, as for any hydrocarbon fuel.

mcqs.stem: Which equation correctly represents the complete combustion of ethanol?

options.text: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
options.rationale: Two carbon, six hydrogen and seven oxygen atoms on each side, counting the oxygen atom in the ethanol.

options.text: C₂H₅OH + 2O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
options.rationale: Balances only the oxygen from the air, ignoring the oxygen atom already in the alcohol.

options.text: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O
options.rationale: Counts only the five hydrogen atoms written before the OH, so a water molecule is lost.

options.text: C₂H₆ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
options.rationale: Burns ethane rather than ethanol: the oxygen atom has been dropped from the formula of the fuel, and the oxygen atoms no longer balance.

mcqs.stem: What happens when ethanol is added to water?

options.text: It dissolves, giving an alkaline solution
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read -OH as hydroxide and expect an alkali.

options.text: It dissolves, giving an acidic solution
options.rationale: Comes from confusing the -OH group with the -COOH group of a carboxylic acid.

options.text: It does not dissolve, forming a layer
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume all organic liquids are immiscible with water.

options.text: It dissolves, giving a neutral solution
options.rationale: Alcohols dissolve in water and the solution formed is neutral.

mcqs.stem: Ethanol is warmed with an oxidising agent. What is formed?

options.text: ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid
options.rationale: An oxidising agent oxidises an alcohol to the carboxylic acid with the same carbon number.

options.text: carbon dioxide and water only
options.rationale: Assumes oxidation must go all the way to the combustion products.

options.text: an ester called ethyl ethanoate
options.rationale: The product of an acid with an alcohol, not of an alcohol with an oxidising agent.

options.text: ethene plus water vapour only
options.rationale: Reverses the addition of water instead of oxidising the alcohol.

mcqs.stem: Which statement gives main uses of the first four alcohols?

options.text: They are used as fuels and as solvents
options.rationale: Fuels and solvents are the main uses of these alcohols, alongside ethanol's use in drinks.

options.text: They are only ever used in alcoholic drinks
options.rationale: Takes the everyday meaning of 'alcohol' as the whole of the chemistry.

options.text: They are all used to make alcoholic drinks
options.rationale: Assumes every member of the series behaves like ethanol; methanol is toxic.

options.text: They are used as fertilisers and as dyes
options.rationale: Chosen by students guessing at industrial uses without a reason to link them to alcohols.

mcqs.stem: How are aqueous solutions of ethanol produced from sugar?

options.text: Sugar solutions are boiled with a catalyst
options.rationale: Applies the idea that more heat always means more product to a process run by living yeast.

options.text: Sugar solutions are fermented using yeast
options.rationale: The specification states that aqueous solutions of ethanol are produced when sugar solutions are fermented using yeast.

options.text: Sugar solutions are electrolysed in a cell
options.rationale: Imports a technique used to extract elements from ionic compounds into an organic process.

options.text: Sugar solutions are neutralised by an acid
options.rationale: Falls back on neutralisation as the reaction type for any mixture in solution.

mcqs.stem: Which conditions are used for the fermentation of sugar using yeast?

options.text: hot, in solution, with air bubbled through
options.rationale: Chosen by students applying the rate rule that hotter is always faster.

options.text: warm, in solution, with no air present
options.rationale: Fermentation uses yeast with sugar in solution at about 30 °C in the absence of oxygen.

options.text: warm and dry, with oxygen kept available
options.rationale: Assumes living yeast must be supplied with air, as in aerobic respiration.

options.text: cold and dry, with no yeast added at all
options.rationale: Removes the yeast, without which no fermentation happens at all.

mcqs.stem: Which of these compounds is an alcohol?

options.text: CH₃COOH
options.rationale: Ends in the letters O and H, but the group is -COOH, so it is a carboxylic acid.

options.text: C₂H₅COOH
options.rationale: Chosen by students who see the O-H inside -COOH and read it as an alcohol group.

options.text: C₃H₇OH
options.rationale: An -OH group on the end of a hydrocarbon chain is the alcohol functional group.

options.text: C₄H₈
options.rationale: An alkene: it contains no oxygen at all, so it cannot be an alcohol.

mcqs.stem: A student says that propanoic acid must be an alcohol. Why is this wrong?

options.text: It is an alcohol; only the name is different here
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read the shared 'propan' stem as fixing the type of compound.

options.text: It contains an O–H bond, so it is an alcohol too
options.rationale: Spots the O-H inside the acid group and treats a part of the group as the whole.

options.text: Its functional group is –COOH, not –OH alone
options.rationale: The whole -COOH group defines a carboxylic acid; an alcohol has -OH joined to a carbon chain.

options.text: It has three carbon atoms, so it must be an alkane
options.rationale: Uses the carbon count rather than the functional group to classify the compound.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is true of the first four carboxylic acids?

options.text: Each contains the functional group –COOH
options.rationale: The specification states that carboxylic acids have the functional group -COOH.

options.text: Each contains the functional group –OH only
options.rationale: Chosen by students who see the O-H in the acid group and stop there.

options.text: Each has a carbon–carbon double bond in it
options.rationale: Imports the alkene functional group into the carboxylic acids.

options.text: Each is unable to react with any carbonate
options.rationale: Chosen by students unsure which acid reactions apply to organic acids.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives the first four members of the homologous series of carboxylic acids?

options.text: ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic, pentanoic
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect the series to begin at the two-carbon member.

options.text: methanoic, ethanoic, propanol, butanol
options.rationale: Mixes in alcohol names, because the stems of the two series are the same.

options.text: methane, ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic
options.rationale: Begins with the alkane methane, from students who confuse the -ane and -oic acid endings.

options.text: methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic
options.rationale: These are the four carboxylic acids named in the specification, in order of increasing carbon number.

mcqs.stem: Ethanoic acid can be represented as CH₃COOH. What does this representation show?

options.text: One carbon atom joined to an acid group
options.rationale: Reads CH₃ as separate from the acid group's carbon atom, giving the wrong carbon count.

options.text: A hydroxide ion joined onto the molecule
options.rationale: Treats the letters OH at the end of the formula as an OH- ion.

options.text: Two carbon atoms, with –COOH on one of them
options.rationale: One carbon atom carries three hydrogen atoms; the other is the carbon atom of the acid group.

options.text: An –OH group only, just as an alcohol has
options.rationale: Reads the O-H inside the acid group as the alcohol functional group.

mcqs.stem: What does a fully displayed formula of ethanoic acid show that CH₃COOH does not?

options.text: How many atoms of each element are present
options.rationale: Already given by CH₃COOH, so it cannot be the additional information.

options.text: Only the chain of carbon atoms in the molecule
options.rationale: Describes the shortcut drawing that leaves hydrogen atoms out.

options.text: Every bond, including the C=O in the acid group
options.rationale: A displayed formula draws all bonds, so the double bond to one oxygen atom is visible.

options.text: The charge carried by each of the atoms
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe the molecule contains ions.

mcqs.stem: Ethanoic acid is added to sodium carbonate. What happens?

options.text: Carbon dioxide gas is given off
options.rationale: A carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate in the same way as any acid, giving carbon dioxide.

options.text: Hydrogen gas is given off
options.rationale: Applies the acid-plus-metal result to a carbonate.

options.text: An ester forms as an oily layer
options.rationale: The product of an acid with an alcohol, not with a carbonate.

options.text: No visible change is seen
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume organic acids are too weak to react at all.

mcqs.stem: What happens when ethanoic acid dissolves in water?

options.text: An alkaline solution with a pH above 7 forms
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read the O-H in the acid group as a hydroxide.

options.text: A salt and water are formed in the solution
options.rationale: Applies neutralisation to a substance simply dissolving.

options.text: An acidic solution with a pH below 7 forms
options.rationale: Carboxylic acids dissolve in water to produce acidic solutions.

options.text: A neutral solution with a pH of exactly 7 forms
options.rationale: Comes from thinking a weak acid barely counts as an acid at all.

mcqs.stem: Ethanoic acid is reacted with ethanol. What is formed?

options.text: an ester called ethyl ethanoate
options.rationale: Carboxylic acids react with alcohols to produce esters.

options.text: a salt plus water, as in neutralisation
options.rationale: Applies the acid-plus-base rule to an alcohol, which is not a base.

options.text: carbon dioxide and water are formed
options.rationale: Expects the carbonate result from any reaction of an acid.

options.text: an alcohol with a longer carbon chain
options.rationale: Assumes the two molecules simply join to extend the chain.

mcqs.stem: Why is ethanoic acid described as a weak acid?

options.text: Its solutions are always very dilute ones
options.rationale: Confuses the strength of an acid with its concentration.

options.text: Its solutions have a pH greater than 7
options.rationale: Treats 'weak' as meaning not acidic; a weak acid still has a pH below 7.

options.text: Only some of its molecules ionise in solution
options.rationale: A weak acid is only partially ionised in aqueous solution.

options.text: It contains only one hydrogen atom per molecule
options.rationale: Miscounts the hydrogen atoms and confuses the number with the extent of ionisation.

mcqs.stem: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid have the same concentration. How do their pH values compare?

options.text: The ethanoic acid has the higher pH of the two
options.rationale: Being weak, it is only partly ionised, so its hydrogen ion concentration is lower and its pH higher.

options.text: The ethanoic acid has a pH higher than 7
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think a weak acid is not acidic at all.

options.text: The two acids have exactly the same pH value
options.rationale: Comes from treating equal concentration as meaning equal acidity.

options.text: The ethanoic acid has the lower pH of the two
options.rationale: Reverses the pH scale, a common slip when comparing acid strengths.

mcqs.stem: Which of these formulae is that of a carboxylic acid?

options.text: C₃H₇OH
options.rationale: An alcohol; chosen by students who cannot separate -OH from -COOH.

options.text: C₂H₅COOH
options.rationale: The -COOH group at the end of the formula is the carboxylic acid functional group.

options.text: C₂H₆O
options.rationale: Contains oxygen and hydrogen but no -COOH group; this is the molecular formula of ethanol.

options.text: C₃H₆
options.rationale: An alkene, containing no oxygen at all, so it cannot be a carboxylic acid.

mcqs.stem: Methanoic acid is the first member of the carboxylic acids. What is its formula?

options.text: CH₃COOH
options.rationale: The formula of ethanoic acid, chosen by students who treat CH₃ as the 'meth' part of the name.

options.text: CH₃OH
options.rationale: Methanol; the shared stem leads students to the wrong functional group.

options.text: C₂H₅COOH
options.rationale: Propanoic acid, picked by counting only the carbon atoms outside the acid group.

options.text: HCOOH
options.rationale: Meth- means one carbon atom in the whole molecule, and that carbon atom is the one in the -COOH group.
